Finding the Best Green Lanes in the UK

Ask ten trail riders to name the best green lanes UK riders should tick off and you will get ten different answers, but they will almost all point to the same handful of regions. Britain's legal byway network is not spread evenly. Some counties have a rich stock of recorded Byways Open to All Traffic and unclassified county roads, while others have almost none. This guide walks through the regions worth planning a trip around, but I want to be crystal clear from the outset: I am describing areas and their character, not handing out turn-by-turn routes, because the legal status of individual lanes changes and it is your responsibility to confirm each one before you ride.

Whatever region you choose, the bike underneath you matters. A capable, manageable machine like the Aprilia Tuareg 660 or the ever-popular Yamaha Tenere 700 will make the lanes a pleasure rather than a wrestling match. If you are still deciding, our guide to mid-weight adventure bikes is a good place to start.

Always Check the Rights of Way First

Before any region-by-region tour, the non-negotiable step. There is no national map of legal green lanes you can simply follow. The status of a lane depends on the local Definitive Map, the highway authority's List of Streets, and any Traffic Regulation Orders in force. The most reliable tools for recreational riders are the resources maintained by the Green Lane Association, GLASS, whose Trailwise database records researched lanes and their current legal status. Cross-check against Ordnance Survey mapping, and when a lane's status is unclear, contact the county's rights of way team. A lane that was a legal byway last season may carry a seasonal or permanent TRO this year. If you are new to all this, read our green laning beginner's guide before you plan a single mile.

No region is worth riding illegally. The whole future of green laning rests on riders sticking rigorously to lanes with confirmed public vehicular rights. When in doubt, leave it out.

Wales: The Spiritual Home of UK Laning

Wales is, for many, the finest laning country in Britain. The mid-Wales uplands around the Elan Valley, the Cambrian Mountains and the hills of Powys hold a strong network of legal byways, many of them ancient drove roads that climb high onto open moorland with breathtaking views. The riding is varied, from rocky climbs to grassy tracks, and the scenery is unmatched. The area also pairs beautifully with the tarmac riding covered in our guide to the best motorcycle roads in Wales, so a Welsh trip can blend lanes and legendary A-roads in a single loop. Be mindful that upland Welsh lanes are fragile and can suffer badly in the wet, so choose your conditions carefully.

The Peak District: Classic Byways Under Pressure

The Peak District has a long heritage of green laning and some of the most famous byways in England, including well-known routes over the gritstone moors and limestone dales. It is also, however, one of the most heavily managed areas, with numerous Traffic Regulation Orders closing or seasonally restricting popular lanes precisely because of their popularity. This makes checking current status absolutely essential here. Ride midweek, keep groups small, and treat the area's sensitivity with respect. The Peaks reward the considerate rider and punish the careless one. Combine your laning with the superb tarmac in our guide to the best Peak District motorcycle roads.

Yorkshire and the Dales: Wild and Rewarding

The Yorkshire Dales and the North Yorkshire moors offer some genuinely wild laning, with long, remote tracks crossing open fell country. The sense of space is extraordinary and the lanes here can feel properly adventurous. As ever, the network is a patchwork of legal byways among many bridleways and restricted byways that are off limits to motorcycles, so careful research is vital. The reward for getting it right is some of the most atmospheric riding in England. For the road connections, our guide to Yorkshire Dales motorcycle routes will help you stitch a full day together.

The South West and Salisbury Plain Fringe

The South West of England, taking in parts of the Wiltshire downs and the wider countryside around the Salisbury Plain area, holds a good number of chalk-track byways with a very different character to the rocky uplands of Wales and the North. These are flowing, fast-drying tracks across open farmland and downland, often making them a sensible choice after wet weather when upland lanes are too fragile to ride. A word of caution specific to this area: the military training estate on Salisbury Plain itself is not a free-for-all, and much of it is restricted or has its own access rules, so confirm status with particular care here. Devon, too, has a famous stock of deep, hedge-lined lanes for those who enjoy tighter, more technical riding.

Lake District Fringes and the North West

The Lake District National Park itself is heavily restricted, with many former lanes now closed to vehicles, so the honest advice is to look to the fringes rather than the honeypot centre. The Cumbrian hills and the country around the park's edges hold some legal byways, but this is an area where the balance has tipped firmly towards restriction and the number of ridable lanes is limited. Research is everything, and expectations should be modest. Riders often combine a modest amount of Lakes-fringe laning with the outstanding road riding the region is famous for.

A Note on Scotland

Scotland deserves special mention because its access laws are entirely different. The much-celebrated Scottish outdoor access rights, sometimes loosely called the right to roam, do not extend to motor vehicles. There is no general right to ride a motorcycle off the public road network in Scotland, and the legal green lane network as understood in England and Wales largely does not exist there. What Scotland offers the trail rider is a small number of legal unsurfaced public roads and tracks, which must be individually confirmed, alongside truly world-class tarmac touring covered in our guide to the best motorcycle roads in Scotland. Do not assume an English or Welsh laning mindset works north of the border.

Planning a Legal Laning Trip

Whichever region calls to you, the process is the same. Join GLASS, research your lanes on Trailwise, cross-check with the local authority, check for TROs, and ride considerately in small groups. Sort your kit with our green laning gear essentials, and if you want to link regions into a bigger adventure, look at our overview of the best adventure motorcycle routes in the UK and the Trans Euro Trail UK section. The best green lane is always the one you have confirmed is legal, ridden with respect, and left exactly as you found it.
keyTakeaways: Britain's legal byway network is uneven; the best laning clusters in specific regions rather than everywhere.
Wales, especially the mid-Wales uplands, is the spiritual home of UK laning, with ancient drove roads.
The Peak District has famous byways but heavy Traffic Regulation Orders, so checking current status is essential.
Always confirm each lane's legal status via GLASS Trailwise, OS mapping and the local highway authority before riding.
Scotland's access laws differ: there is no general right to ride off the public road network there.

faq.a: Wales is, for many, the finest laning country in Britain. The most reliable tools are the Green Lane Association's resources, especially the Trailwise database. Cross-check against Ordnance Survey mapping, and when a lane's status is unclear, contact the county's rights of way team.

Checking current status is absolutely essential here. Ride midweek, keep groups small, and treat the area's sensitivity with respect.

faq.q: Where can I ride after wet weather?
faq.a: The South West, taking in parts of the Wiltshire downs and the countryside around Salisbury Plain, holds chalk-track byways that are fast-drying and flowing, making them a sensible choice when upland lanes are too fragile. Note that the military training estate on Salisbury Plain itself is restricted with its own access rules, so confirm status with particular care there.

faq.q: Can I green lane in Scotland?
